question.prompt: A majority of the \(30\) students in Ms. Demeanor’s class bought pencils at the school bookstore. Each of these students bought the same number of pencils, and this number was greater than \(1.\) The cost of a pencil in cents was greater than the number of pencils each student bought, and the total cost of all the pencils was \(\$17.71.\) What was the cost of a pencil in cents?

solutions.explanation:
Use the whole-cent retail pricing convention recorded in the packet. Let \(n\) be the number of students buying pencils, \(k\) the number each buys, and \(p\) the price of one pencil in cents. These are positive integers.

A majority of \(30\) students means \(16\le n\le30\). The other conditions give \(1<k<p\). Converting the total to cents yields
\[
nkp=1771=7\cdot11\cdot23.
\]
In particular, \(n\) must divide \(1771\). Each positive divisor is a product of a selection of the three distinct prime factors \(7,11,23\). A divisor using two or more of them is at least \(7\cdot11=77\), so the only divisor between \(16\) and \(30\) is \(23\). Thus \(n=23\), leaving
\[
kp=\frac{1771}{23}=77.
\]
The positive factor pairs of \(77\), with the smaller factor first, are \((1,77)\) and \((7,11)\). Since \(1<k<p\), only \(k=7\) and \(p=11\) work.

Indeed, \(23\) is a majority of \(30\), each student buys \(7>1\) pencils, and \(11>7\). Their total cost is \(23\cdot7\cdot11=1771\) cents. Under the stated convention, the price is \(11\) cents, choice B.
